titleStmt.title: Shiji 史记 · 秦庄襄王三年: notes

div.interp: The third year of King Zhuangxiang of Qin, 247 BC.

The Jijie cites Xu Guang: one text has 波 for 汲, Bo County being also in Henei. The Zhengyi cites the Kuodizhi: the old city of Gaodu is Zezhou; the old city of Ji lies twenty-five li south-west of the Ji County governed from Weizhou.

The Zhengyi cites the Kuodizhi: Yuci is a County of Bingzhou, the ancient Yuci; Xincheng, also called Xiaopingcheng, lies forty-seven li south-west of Shanyang County in Shuozhou; the old city of Langmeng twenty-six li north-east of Yangqu County in Bingzhou. The Table and the Hereditary Houses enter the campaign under the previous year (248 BC, §2, §3).
The Zhengyi: the thirty-seven Fortresses are the lands of the three States of Bingzhou, Daizhou and Shuozhou, in the names of the Tang.
四月日食: the Table enters an eclipse under the previous year (248 BC, §2).
王龁: the Basic Annals' writing of the general whom the Table (§2) and the Suiji call 王齮, Wang Yi; the two are taken as one man.
The Zhengyi: Shangdang had again turned against Qin, hence the attack.
The Zhengyi: all north of Shangdang is Taiyuan land, that is the thirty-seven Fortresses above. The Hereditary House of Yan puts the founding under the previous year (248 BC, §3).
The Zhengyi: Wuji is Lord Xinling; he led the troops of Yan, Zhao, Han, Chu and Wei against Qin.
The Zhengyi: Meng Ao, beaten by the five states' troops, broke off and fell back to Hewai, the States of Shanzhou and Huazhou in the names of the Tang.
子政: Ying Zheng, King of Qin from this accession; the Basic Annals name him by the imperial title he took later.
王齮: the Basic Annals (§1) write 王龁 for the same general.
The Zhengyi on the Basic Annals names them: Yan, Zhao, Han, Chu and Wei (§1). The Table's second Qin line and its Wei line record the same battle from the two sides.
The sixteenth year of King Kaolie of Chu, 247 BC.
赵政: the First Emperor by his clan name Zhao, as the Chu house writes him; born in Zhao, he was of the Zhao clan of the Ying line.
The nineteenth year of King Xiaocheng of Zhao, 247 BC.
易土: the Suoyin gives the pronunciation of 易 as that of 亦 and glosses it as exchanging Counties with Yan. The commentaries' placing of the six towns is in their entries.
The thirtieth year of King Anxi of Wei, 247 BC. The Prince's return and the battle are told at length in his Biography, 256 BC §4.
或: the Suoyin notes that the Zhanguoce has Su Qin speaking for Prince Zeng.
公孙喜: the Suoyin notes that the Zhanguoce writes Gongsun Yan 公孙衍.
The twenty-sixth year of King Huanhui of Han, 247 BC.

公子: the Biography calls Wuji "the Prince" throughout. The passage, from his stay in Zhao to the historian's judgement, is the one already given under 256 BC (§4), repeated here for the year it dates: the thirtieth year of King Anxi, 247 BC, of his return and the victory at Hewai.
The King of Qin of the slander is King Zhuangxiang, in whose last year the Prince took command; the four years of drinking and the Prince's death fall under King Zheng.

247 BC, this year; the Basic Annals (§1) give the day, Bingwu of the fifth month. The Jijie cites Xu Guang: Zheng was then thirteen. The two Biographies run on from this point far past the year: the matter of Lao Ai falls in the king's early years and ends with Ai's revolt and death in 238 BC and Buwei's fall in 237 BC; Li Si's memorial is dated by the Zhengyi to the king's tenth year, 237 BC, and his Biography closes with the unification of 221 BC. The passages are given whole here, where the chronology meets them.
仲父: the Zhengyi: 仲 is 中, the middle; a second father; on the model of Duke Huan of Qi, who made Guan Zhong his 仲父.

The Zhengyi, from the Table: Lord Pingyuan died in King Zhaoxiang's fifty-sixth year (251 BC), Lord Xinling in the First Emperor's fourth (243 BC), and Li Yuan killed Lord Chunshen in his ninth (238 BC); Lord Mengchang died after King Zhaoxiang's twenty-fourth year (283 BC), the earliest of the four. The Suoyin cites Wang Shao, "Mengchang and Chunshen had long been dead", and answers that by the Table and the Biographies Mengchang and Pingyuan died somewhat earlier, but Xinling's command of the five states against Qin at Hewai falls in King Zhuangxiang's reign, when Buwei was already Chancellor, and Chunshen and Buwei were contemporaries, each Chancellor for over ten years, so that he cannot be said to have been long dead.

八览、六论、十二纪: the Suoyin names the eight Surveys (有始, 孝行, 慎大, 先识, 审分, 审应, 离俗, 时君), the six Discourses (开春, 慎行, 贵直, 不苟, 以顺, 士容) and the twelve Records, one for each month, beginning with 孟春; the two hundred thousand-odd words make twenty-six juan.
吕氏春秋: Master Lü's Spring and Autumn Annals, the compilation of Lü Buwei's retainers in twenty-six juan; quoted under 256 BC (§7).

The Suoyin: the Dilizhi's Weicheng County in Youfufeng is the old Xianyang, renamed Xincheng by Emperor Gao and Weicheng by Emperor Jing; 咸 means "all", the place lying north of the Wei and south of the northern slope, on the 阳 side of both water and hill.
始皇帝: the Biography names the young king by his later title.
桐轮: the Zhengyi: a small cart wheel made of tong wood.
腐罪: the Zhengyi: 腐 is read fu; the palace punishment, 宫刑, of the convict.
The Zhengyi: the old city of Yong lies seven li south of Yong County in Qizhou, with the Da Zheng Palace of the Qin capital.

The Suoyin: the Dilizhi's Shangcai County in Runan, "the old state of Cai, fief of Shu Du, King Wu of Zhou's brother; at the eighteenth generation Marquis Ping moved to Xincai", both in Runan; two generations later Marquis Zhao moved to Xiacai, in Pei; in the time of the Six States it was Chu land, hence "Shangcai of Chu".
郡小吏: the Suoyin: a petty clerk of a district 乡小史; Liu: in charge of the district's documents.

游者主事: the Suoyin: in an age when the lords of ten thousand chariots contend for mastery, the travelling persuaders can win merit and fame and are given charge of affairs; Liu's reading, "travel among the Lords and seek a strong master to serve", twists the text and is wrong.
秋: the Zhengyi: in autumn all things ripen; in a time of contention the persuaders too are ripe.

禽鹿视肉: the Suoyin: 禽鹿 means birds and beasts, which know only to stare at meat and eat it; the Zhuangzi and Master Su say "a man who does not learn is like one who stares at meat and eats", and Yang Xiong's Fayan "a man who does not learn, how does he differ from a beast?"; one who cannot persuade and win honour is as the beasts, having a man's face and able only to walk upright.
诟: the Zhengyi: read hou; shame.

非世: the Suoyin: 非 is to censure, the "unbridled discourse of men out of office". The Zhengyi: to censure the age's wealth and rank, to hate its honours and gains and entrust oneself to inaction is not the gentleman's true feeling; it is that his strength cannot attain them.
247 BC: the point at which Li Si's story meets this year. What follows, his rise under King Zheng and the memorial of 237 BC, belongs to the following years.

胥人者，去其几也: the Suoyin: 胥人 is like 胥吏, petty men; 去 is to lose; 几 is the first stirring of movement; the gentleman sees the stirring and acts without waiting out the day, while the petty man does not know the moment of stirring and so always loses his time; Liu's gloss of 几 as "strong" is wrong. The Zhengyi reads 胥 as 相, "mutually", and 几 as 察, "to examine": the Six States east of the Pass stand against Qin as rivals, and the secret affairs of their rulers and ministers all have flaws by which great deeds may be achieved if one bears with them ruthlessly.
因瑕衅而遂忍之: the Suoyin: where the Lords have flaws, steel the heart and cut them away; "so I shall urge Qin to annex the world".
六世: the Zhengyi: Duke Xiao, Duke Huiwen, King Wu, King Zhao, King Xiaowen and King Zhuangxiang.
灶上骚除: the Jijie cites Xu Guang, 骚 read as 埽; the Suoyin: Qin's annexing of the world would be like the cook sweeping the dirt from the stove top, no difficulty at all.

注溉渠: the Zhengyi: the Zheng Guo canal rose twenty-five li south-west of Yunyang County in Yongzhou, drawn from Zhongshan westward at Hukou, and ran along the northern hills east into the Luo, three hundred-odd li, to water the fields; Han, hard pressed by Qin's arms, sent the water engineer Zheng Guo to spy on Qin by building the canal, to waste its labour and keep it from attacking eastward.

一切逐客: the Suoyin: 一切 is "as one rule", to expel them all; 切 is as a sharp knife cutting, one stroke of the axe severing everything; those who gloss 一切 in the Hanshu as "for the time being" have not got it.
The Zhengyi: in the First Emperor's tenth year (237 BC). The memorial is the 谏逐客书, the remonstrance against the expulsion of the guests.
缪公: Duke Mu 穆公 as the memorial writes him.

The Suoyin: the Basic Annals of Qin say Duke Xian of Jin sent Baili Xi to Qin as a bride-servant with Duke Mu's wife; Xi fled to Wan, and rustics of Chu seized him. The Zhengyi cites the Xinxu: Baili Xi, a man of Wan in Chu, served in Yu; when Yu fell he entered Qin, and was called the Grand Master of the Five Rams' Skins.

The Suoyin: the Basic Annals also have Baili Xi tell Duke Mu, "I am not the equal of my friend Jian Shu, who is worthy but unknown to the age", whereupon the duke welcomed him with rich gifts and made him Senior Grand Master; "from Song" has no known source. The Zhengyi cites the Kuodizhi: Jian Shu was a man of Qizhou, then travelling in Song, hence welcomed from Song.

The Suoyin: Pi Bao's flight from Jin to Qin is plain in the Zuo Tradition; Gongsun Zhi is Zi Sang, a Grand Master of Qin, and his coming from Jin has no known source. The Zhengyi cites the Kuodizhi: Gongsun Zhi was a man of Qizhou who travelled in Jin and later returned to Qin.

并国二十: the Suoyin: the Basic Annals say Duke Mu, on You Yu's counsel, attacked the king of the Rong, added twelve states and opened a thousand li of land, becoming hegemon over the Western Rong; here the merits of all five are summed, hence "twenty"; texts that alter it to "twelve" are wrong.

The Suoyin: in King Hui's time Zhang Yi, as Chancellor, asked to attack Han and send troops down to Sanchuan to menace the two Zhou; Sima Cuo asked to attack Shu, the king agreed, and Shu was destroyed; after Yi's death King Wu wished to open the road to Sanchuan and had Gan Mao take Yiyang. All is credited to Zhang Yi here because he was Chancellor of Qin, and because he first asked to attack Sanchuan.
The Zhengyi: in King Hui's tenth year (328 BC) Wei ceded the fifteen Counties of Shang Commandery.
The Zhengyi: in King Hui's thirteenth year (of his second reckoning, 312 BC) Qin attacked Chu's Hanzhong and took six hundred li of land.

九夷: the Suoyin: the Yi belonging to Chu; the Dilizhi's Jiangling County in Nan Commandery is "the old Ying, capital of Chu", and its Yicheng County "the old Yan". The Zhengyi: the Yi are the annexing of Ba and Shu, the gathering in of Shang Commandery, the taking of Hanzhong and the attacks on Yiqu and Danli; the Nine Yi are properly the nine kinds of Eastern Yi, and the phrase is a figure of style.
The Zhengyi: Sishui County 氾水县 of Henan 河南府, in the names of the Tang.
华阳: Lord Huayang 华阳君, Mi Rong. The Jijie cites Xu Guang: 华 in one text 叶.
蚕食: the Suoyin cites Gao You on the Huainanzi: to eat up, leaving nothing.
The Zhengyi: Kungang lies four hundred li north-east of the state of Khotan (于阗), and the ridge yields jade.

随、和之宝: the pearl of the Marquis of Sui and the jade disc of Bian He. The Zhengyi cites the Kuodizhi: Mount Fen, also called Kunshan and Duanshe Hill, "the hill of the severed snake", lies twenty-five li north of Sui County in Suizhou; the Shuoyuan: the Marquis of Sui on a journey met a great snake cut in two and, suspecting it was uncanny, had it dressed with medicine; the snake was able to go, and the place was named for it; after a year the snake brought him a bright pearl an inch across, pure white and shining, called the pearl of Sui. The disc of Bian He the First Emperor made the seal of state handed down.
太阿: the Jijie: see the Biography of Su Qin. The Suoyin cites the Yuejueshu: the King of Chu summoned Ou Yezi and Gan Jiang to make three iron swords, Ganjiang, Moye and Tai'e.
纤离: the Jijie cites Xu Guang: Xianli and Pushao are both names of fine horses; the Suoyin: both horse names, Xu following the Sunqingzi.
灵鼍之鼓: the Jijie cites Zheng Xuan on the Yueling: alligator hide can be stretched over drums.
駃騠: the Suoyin gives the reading jue-ti; the Zhoushu, "the true north offers jueti"; the Guangya, "a kind of horse"; Guo Pu on the Shanglin fu, "born three days and it outruns its mother".
西蜀: Shu, the Chengdu plain.
下陈: the Suoyin: the rear ranks; Master Yan, "I have two daughters and wish to have them enter among the lower ranks".

宛珠之簪，傅玑之珥: the Suoyin: 宛 read yuan, to wind pearls round the hairpin; 傅 read fu; 傅玑 is to set seed-pearls on the ear-pendant, 珥 being the ear-plug and 玑 a pearl that is not round; or 宛珠 is the pearl of Sui, Sui lying south of the Han and Wan near it; women's ornaments, none of them things Qin possesses.
阿缟: the Jijie cites Xu Guang: Dong'e County of Qi, whence silks come.
随俗雅化: the Jijie cites Xu Guang, 随俗 in one text 修使; the Suoyin: refined and adaptable, able to suit the common taste.
击甕叩缶: the Suoyin cites the Shuowen: 甕 a water jar; 缶 an earthen vessel, which the men of Qin beat to keep time to music.
昭、虞、武、象: the Jijie cites Xu Guang, 昭 in one text 韶; the dances of Shun, of King Wu and the Xiang.

太山: Mount Tai. The Suoyin cites the Guanzi, "the sea does not refuse water and so achieves its greatness; the mountain does not refuse earth and stones and so achieves its height", and the Wenzi, "the sage does not refuse the words of the firewood-carrier, and so widens his name".
资: the Suoyin: 给, to supply.
藉寇兵而赍盗粮: the Suoyin gives the readings and cites the Shuowen, 赍 is to carry and present; 赍 or 资, the sense the same.
The Jijie cites the Xinxu: Si, among those expelled, submitted his memorial of remonstrance on the road; it reached the First Emperor, who sent men after him as far as Liyi and brought him back.
The unification of 221 BC and the imperial title; the Biography's summary runs to the end of the First Emperor's reign.

The rescue of Zhao was in 257 BC (told under 256 BC, §4), so "twenty-odd years after" would fall in the 230s; but the Jijie on the passage cites Xu Guang, by the Table, placing Tian Dan's attack on Liaocheng ten-odd years after Changping (260 BC), that is in the 240s, and the Suoyin notes that the "thirty-odd years" of some texts is an error. The compiler enters the three items here with their date left open.
The passage follows Lu Zhonglian's refusal to let Zhao honour Qin as Emperor during the siege of Handan; the relief of Zhao is told under 256 BC (§4).

The Jijie cites Xu Guang: by the Table, Tian Dan's attack on Liaocheng is ten-odd years after Changping. The Suoyin: Xu Guang, following the Table, puts it ten-odd years after Changping; the reading "thirty-odd years" is wrong. The Zhengyi on Liaocheng: now a County of Bozhou, in the names of the Tang.
却死: the Suoyin: to avoid death.

The Suoyin on Qi's Nanyang: Qi's lands north of the Huai and on the Si; on Pinglu: a town on the western border, and the Zhengyi: a County of Yanzhou in the names of the Tang; on Jibei: the land of Liaocheng. The Zhengyi: Qi has no mind to attack Chu and Wei to the south, holding the harm at Nanyang and Pinglu small beside the gain of Liaocheng, which it will surely attack.
衡秦之势成: the Suoyin: Qin and Qi were at peace at this time, hence the phrase.

The Suoyin: Qi gives up the lands on the Si that Chu attacked, cuts off the right-hand land that Wei attacked, Pinglu, leaving it unrelieved, and bends its purpose to attacking Liaocheng and settling Jibei.
交退: the Suoyin: 交 is "both"; earlier Chu attacked Nanyang and Wei Pinglu; now both armies have withdrawn and Yan's relief does not come, so the position is perilous.
The Jijie cites Xu Guang: this event is ten years from Changping. Li Fu's defeat by Zhao and the siege of Yan are told under 251 BC.
The Zhengyi: as Mo Di defended Song and repulsed the Chu army.
The Zhengyi: Sun Bin could so comfort his soldiers that they had no second thoughts.

资说士: the Suoyin: having nourished the people, he also furnishes the persuaders, aiming in the end at a strong state; Liu reads 说士 as 锐士, "crack troops", which is plausible but it is better to keep the character.
矫国更俗: the Suoyin: he wishes the general of Yan to return to Yan, set the state's affairs right and reform its corrupt customs.
亡意: the Suoyin: 亡 is read wu, "none": if you have no mind at all to return to Yan, then abandon Yan and go east to Qi.

陶、卫: the Suoyin: Yan Du's note on the Zhanguoce takes Tao as Tao Zhu Gong and Wey as Prince Jing of Wey, wrongly; Wang Shao: Wei Ran was enfeoffed at Tao and Lord Shang was surnamed Wey, and the comparison is with these. Neither is tagged, the names standing for the men.
称孤: 孤, "the orphan", is the self-designation of the ruler of a state; to call oneself so is to rule.
遗公子纠: the Suoyin: 遗 is to abandon, abandoning Prince Jiu to serve Xiaobai. The Zhengyi: Guan Zhong was Tutor to Prince Jiu, whom Lu killed; not following him in death was cowardice.
臧获: the Jijie cites the Fangyan: between Jing and the Huai, the sea and Mount Dai, Yan and Qi, a male slave is abused as 臧 and a female as 获.

The Zhengyi: Duke Huan of Qi was the first to receive from King Xiang of Zhou the sacrificial meat of Kings Wen and Wu, the red bow and arrows and the great carriage, hence first of the Five Hegemons.
曹子: the Suoyin: the Lu general Cao Mei 曹昧, that is Cao Mo 曹沫. His three defeats and the covenant of Ke fall under Duke Zhuang of Lu, 681 BC.
枝桓公之心: the Suoyin: 枝 is 拟, to point at.
漢簡: the compiler does not say which slips.
246 BC. The Basic Annals of the First Emperor: "In the first year Jinyang revolted; the general Meng Ao attacked and settled it." The item will be met under that year.
